title: Ring Buffer Documentation/Example
last_maintainer_comment: @acidtonic No, I don't think a ring buffer would be appropriate for your case. The ring buffer is a very specific data structure. It's good when you have one thread writing some data (the producer) and another thread reading the data (the consumer) and you want that access to be lock-free. It's useful in audio because you'll sometimes end up in a situation where you have some capturing thread writing to the ring buffer, while at the same time on a different thread you have something that is consuming that data. It allows those two threads to be completely decoupled. In your case I would consider just using a standard old buffer.

title: Documentation?
last_maintainer_comment: > So would it be performance problem if I want to ma_device_init new device every time I play a sound and then ma_device_uninit it? Don't do that. This will never be efficient, even if you were to use WASAPI, ALSA, PulseAudio, etc. directly. Instead you should initialize a single device instance and keep it alive for as long as you need it. Then do one of two things: 1) Keep the device running at all times and write silence when no sounds are playing; or 2) When no sounds are playing, stop the device with ma_device_stop(), and then when a sound needs to be played restart it with ma_device_start(). Which brings me to the next point... > Of course I could use 1 device but different sound can have different outputSampleRate for example. When you initialize a decoder you can pass in a config object which lets you override the output sample rate. Set the output sample rate of your decoder to the input sample rate of the device, like this: ``` ma_decoder_config config = ma_decoder_config_init( device.playback.format, device.playback.channels, device.sampleRate); result = ma_decoder_init_file("my_file.wav", &decoderConfig, &decoder); ``` This way you can play back your sound files without needing to update any device configuration. > can I have a callback to react when the playback is finished? No. Instead use the return value of ma_decoder_read_pcm_frames() to know whether or not you have reached the end. The return value is the number of PCM frames actually read. When it reaches the end, this will be less than the number of frames you originally requested. > if not, can I receive the duration of a sound decoded by ma_decoder? No. This is due to a limitation with stb_vorbis in push mode which is what I use in miniaudio. I have a TODO to add an API for this, which will just return 0 for the Vorbis backend. No time frame on that just yet. > if not, could you provide a proper example with one sample played 2 times – second time just after first playback is finished? The closest example I have of this is the simple_mixing examples in the examples folder. This will show you how to detect when you've reached the end of the sound file. To restart it just seek back to the start with ma_decoder_seek_to_pcm_frame(&decoder, 0).

title: Seeking on a decoder that's using a non-file-native decode format
last_maintainer_comment: OK, I've pushed a fix for the main issue to the dev branch, however I realised as I was writing this fix that it won't actually fix your scenario completely (though it should sound a bit better). Basically there's no way to get good quality output using the one-decoder technique. The issue is that the internal resampler needs to track state, which includes timing information for interpolation and also previous and future samples for filtering. As you move around with a seek and then read some frames, the internal state will be updated to reflect the new playback position, but then when you seek back to the original location, the original state will not be restored, therefore leading to a glitch. I understand if that may be a bit hard to follow, but basically if you want 100% glitch free audio you can't use a single decoder. I would recommend just using multiple `ma_decoder` instances and be done with it. You can optimize it a bit by loading the file into memory and then using `ma_decoder_init_memory()`, using the same memory location for each call. If that's not suitable, you could also do something more sophisticated and use `ma_decoder_init()` which allows you to implement custom callbacks for data delivery, but that's a much more advanced system which might be more than you need.

title: MP3 distorted in 0.10.7
last_maintainer_comment: Yes, that's expected. If the format of the device does not match the output format of the decoder you'll get bad glitching. The decoder will only decode in the format that you specify in the decoder config, or if you specify NULL for the decoder config (as in the simple_playback example) it'll use it's native format, which for MP3 is probably `ma_format_s16`. The `ma_device` and `ma_decoder` objects are completely decoupled which means miniaudio has no way of knowing how the two objects will be interacting with each other. For this reason, automatic data conversion between decoder and device has never been anything miniaudio has ever done. What you can do, however, is explicitly set the output format of your decoders to the input format of the device (or vice versa, depending your setup) which will result in it just working. My recommendation is to change your program so that *all* decoders have an explicit `ma_decoder_config` passed into `ma_decoder_init_file()`, with the output format specified in `ma_decoder_config` being set to the input format of the device: ```c ma_decoder_config decoderConfig = ma_decoder_config_init( device.playback.format, device.playback.channels, device.sampleRate ); result = ma_decoder_init_file("my_file.wav", &decoderConfig, &decoder); ``` Doing it this way results in the output format of your decoders being set to the input format of the device and everything should just work. Just keep in mind the format if you're doing any kind of mixing or effects processing.

title: Question: playing the same sound simultaneously
last_maintainer_comment: Each time you want to play a sound, even if it's the same underlying sound file, you need a separate `ma_sound` object. You need to not think of it as one `ma_sound` object getting played multiple times simultaneously, but rather for each sound you want to play, you need a new `ma_sound` object. The underlying sound data is reference counted which means the sound file will only be loaded once. One thing you can do is pre-load the necessary sounds like this: ```c ma_sound* pPreLoadedSounds; /* <-- Allocate this array somewhere. */ // In your initialization routine... ma_sound_init_from_file(pEngine, "my_sound.wav", ..., &pPreLoadedSounds[0]); // In your menu stuff. ma_engine_play_sound(pEngine, "my_sound.wav", NULL); /* The last parameter is the group you want to assign the sound to. Can be NULL. */ // In your uninitialization routine... ma_sound_uninit(pPreLoadedSounds[0]); /* <-- Probably run this in a loop for each cached sound. */ ``` In the code above you are pre-loading a sound and just leaving it there. Then, when you call `ma_engine_play_sound()`, which is a fire-and-forget type of function, it won't actually be loading the sound again because the `ma_sound` object you pre-loaded earlier has already loaded it and will be holding a reference to it. The sound that's created internally will just increment the reference count and use the already-loaded data. If you want to do more advanced stuff, such as applying effects, pitch shifting, panning, etc. you'll need to use `ma_sound_init_from_file()` and manually manage your `ma_sound` objects (but keep using the same pre-loading system). I think I'll be adding some helper functions later on to make this a bit more intuitive. I've got some cloning stuff in the pipeline which might make things a bit cleaner.

title: ma_sound_set_start_time_in_pcm_frames() not working
last_maintainer_comment: This is the expected behaviour. The sound still needs to be in a started state in order for it to eventually play. So the correct way to do it is to schedule the start time with `ma_sound_set_start_time_in_pcm_frames()` and then to unmark it as stopped with `ma_sound_start()`: ```c ma_sound_set_start_time_in_pcm_frames(&sound, ma_engine_get_time(&engine) + (ma_engine_get_sample_rate(&engine) * 2)); ma_sound_start(&sound); ``` The specific order of the calls shouldn't matter in practice. Note that the same does not apply for stopping - scheduling a stop without a an explicit `ma_sound_stop()` should work fine. The relevant code that controls this is in `ma_node_get_state_by_time_range()` (a `ma_sound` is a `ma_node`): ```c /* An explicitly stopped node is always stopped. */ if (state == ma_node_state_stopped) { return ma_node_state_stopped; } ``` Understand the confusion with that one. I've added a note about this to the documentation which is in the dev branch now.

In the callback you have this: ```c double* buffArr = *(buffer) + start; ``` That's wrong. Instead you should do something like this: ```c void* buffArr = ma_offset_ptr(*buffer, start * ma_get_bytes_per_frame(pDecoder->outputFormat, pDecoder->outputChannels)); ``` That's assuming `start` is in PCM frames and not bytes, which it looks like it is if I'm reading it correctly. Also, with your buffer allocation: ```c outputBuffer = malloc(buffLength * sizeof(*outputBuffer)); ``` Change that this: ```c outputBuffer = malloc(buffLength * ma_get_bytes_per_frame(pDecoder->outputFormat, pDecoder->outputChannels)); ``` The only reason this wasn't crashing is by coincidence. If you had passed in a file with, say, 4 channels, it would have crashed. So to summarise, as a start I would replace all of your `double*` pointers with `void*` and offset with `ma_offset_ptr()` and `ma_get_bytes_per_frame()`. title: Mirrored memory ring buffer
last_maintainer_comment: This has been done in the dev-0.12 branch. The new ring buffer can accept a caller-allocated buffer to act as the backing store. This buffer can optionally be a mirrored buffer, or it can just be a standard `malloc()` allocation double the size of the ring buffer capacity. I do not have plans to provide a mirrored allocation routine in miniaudio so if you want to use a mirrored buffer you'll need to do that allocation yourself and then pass it into the ring buffer initialization routine and specify the `MA_RING_BUFFER_FLAG_MIRRORED` flag. The new ring buffer is called `ma_ring_buffer` (previously `ma_rb`) and `ma_audio_ring_buffer` (previously `ma_pcm_rb`). The difference between the two is `ma_ring_buffer` is generic and lower level, whereas `ma_audio_ring_buffer` is focused on PCM audio data and is compatible with the `ma_data_source` API. I have updated the documentation with information on how to use it (https://github.com/mackron/miniaudio/commit/f99ff4cec038b5456a2a05a8a66dcaeb9baf0369). In my earlier message I said that I would leave the old ring buffers in place, but I've changed my mind and have decided to delete them.

title: mp3 trial and error significantly slows down ma_sound_init_from_file
last_maintainer_comment: So good news and bad news on this one. The good news is that I've implemented a solution for this. The bad news is that it's in the dev-0.12 branch which means it won't be released for a while. The reason for this is that I've made some API breaking changes so I don't want to release it in the 0.11.x cycle and break anyone's builds. The main change is that you can now configure backend priorities explicitly. I've also removed the extension-checking logic for determining backend prioritization. Now the `encodingFormat` member of `ma_decoder_config` is put to better use in determining an appropriate decoding backend. Decoding backends now report the encoding format they support (`ma_encoding_format_unknown` if they support multiple formats) which miniaudio will use in determining which backend to skip over. This combined with being able to explicitly specify priorities should give you a lot of flexibility. I've tested on my end with the resource manager, and it will now load from the Vorbis backend first before attempting anything, so long as the libvorbis decoder is at the top of the priority list, or `encodingFormat` is set to `ma_encoding_format_vorbis`. Rather than typing everything out again, here's a copy and paste of the release notes I've written up: --- You can now customize the priority of stock decoding backends, with the ability to plug in your own custom decoders, with total control over prioritization of everything. By default, the same prioritization as before will be used, but if you want to configure it, you can do so via the decoder config: const ma_decoding_backend_vtable* ppDecodingBackends[] = { // These are custom backends. ma_decoding_backend_libvorbis, ma_decoding_backend_libopus, // These are stock backends. Any of these that you want to support must be explicitly // listed when specifying a custom list of decoding backends. ma_decoding_backend_wav, ma_decoding_backend_flac, ma_decoding_backend_mp3 }; ma_decoder_config decoderConfig = ma_decoder_config_init_default(); decoderConfig.ppBackendVTables = ppDecodingBackends; decoderConfig.backendCount = sizeof(ppDecodingBackends) / sizeof(ppDecodingBackends[0]); Note that when specifying your list of backends, you *must* list every backend that you want to support, including stock ones. By default, when `ppBackendVTables` is set to NULL, miniaudio will use a default list of stock backends. You can rearrange this list however you like, including mixing up the order. This is a valid priority order, for example. const ma_decoding_backend_vtable* ppDecodingBackends[] = { ma_decoding_backend_wav, // Most of our files are .wav, so make that the highest priority. ma_decoding_backend_libvorbis, // Our music is mostly Vorbis... ma_decoding_backend_mp3 // ... But we also support MP3. }; Notice with the example above that we've excluded flac and libopus. In this case, FLAC files and Opus files will not be supported when trying to load files. Also note how we've mixed up the libvorbis decoder, which is a custom decoder, within the stock decoders. You configure this prioritization however you like. Previously when miniaudio initialized a decoder from a file path it would use the file extension as a hint to determine which of the stock backends to try first. This logic has been removed, but there are tools to allow you to achieve the same effect. Decoding backends now implement a new callback called `onGetEncodingFormat`. This is used to determine the encoding format the decoder supports (if it supports more than one, `ma_encoding_format_unknown` is used). This combined with the `encodingFormat` member of `ma_decoder_config` allows miniaudio to quickly skip over any decoding backend that cannot possibly decode that file. You can use it like this: decoderConfig.encodingFormat = ma_encoding_format_from_path(pFilePath); The `ma_encoding_format_from_path()` function uses the file extension to determine the encoding format. If the extension is not recognized by miniaudio, `ma_encoding_format_unknown` will be used in which case miniaudio will use it's standard prioritization rules as explained above. You do not need to use `ma_encoding_format_from_path()` if you don't want to. If, for example, you know that the file will be a wav file, you could just use `ma_encoding_format_wav` directly. If you don't like the `decoderConfig.encodingFormat` system, another option is to simply specify only a single decoding backend in your backend list: const ma_decoding_backend_vtable* ppDecodingBackends[] = { ma_decoding_backend_wav, // All of our files are .wav }; For authors of custom backends, you should implement the new `onGetEncodingFormat` callback. See the miniaudio_libvorbis.h and miniaudio_libopus.h files in the extras folder for an example. If you're unsure, just have it return `ma_encoding_format_unknown`.

title: How can I Cache ma_sound's into memory?
last_maintainer_comment: miniaudio supports reference counting. You can just initialize a `ma_sound` object and hold onto it for as long as you need. That way the reference count will never hit 0 and will never be unloaded. However, your map is wrong. You need to remember this trip hazard from the documentation: > In miniaudio, objects are transparent structures. Unlike many other libraries, there are no handles to opaque objects which means you need to allocate memory for objects yourself. In the examples presented in this documentation you will often see objects declared on the stack. You need to be careful when translating these examples to your own code so that you don't accidentally declare your objects on the stack and then cause them to become invalid once the function returns. **In addition, you must ensure the memory address of your objects remain the same throughout their lifetime. You therefore cannot be making copies of your objects.** So any time you add a new entry to your `std::map` you're not only making a copy of your `ma_sound`, it's possible that the internal memory is being moved around which is violating the rule that your `ma_sound` object must maintain the same address in memory for it's lifetime. Instead you should store pointers to your `ma_sound` objects and allocate the memory of your individual `ma_sound` objects on the heap. Then your map becomes `std::map<std::string, ma_sound*>`.

If your sound has already been decoded, you can use `ma_audio_buffer` instead of `ma_decoder`. A `ma_sound_init_from_memory()` is planned for the future. You do not need to use the resource manager or any FLAC-specific stuff. The resource manager is all about loading from files, and the FLAC stuff is an implementation detail and should not be used directly.

One of those two things need to account for the channel count which you are not doing.

title: Lack of error handling in WAV files
last_maintainer_comment: I have no intention on changing this. The only practical way to know the exact frame count is to fully decode the file in some kind of pre-processing phase which has two problems: 1) Initialization overhead; 2) It would break down for things like internet streams where there is no real notion of an end. Bear in mind that the `ma_decoder` API is more than just regular WAV files sitting on disk. The correct usage is to check the returned value from `ma_decoder_read_pcm_frames()` to know when the end of the file has been reached and how many frames were read. You should not be depending on `ma_decoder_get_length_in_pcm_frames()` for your actual decoding logic. It exists for people who can make use of it as a hint or are using trusted input. I've added a note in my todo list to add a mention that `ma_decoder_read_pcm_frames()` is read from metadata and should not be considered 100% accurate for untrusted input.

title: Possible problem choosing mono mic on Windows
last_maintainer_comment: > You advise to always assume mono if mono is requested, but in general across the audio platforms I will be porting to ( Windows, OSX, iOS and Android ) when my software sets out its preferences for channel count, sample rate, sample period and so on, isn't it true that it can't assume its stated preferences will be supported on the relevant platform and/or particular device? miniaudio will do the necessary conversion for you automatically. > So my policy has always been to want to check the parameter values the hardware actually assigns in response to my requests. You can do that by setting the device count to zero in the device config: ``` deviceConfig.capture.channels = 0; // <-- Tells miniaudio to use the native channel count ``` Then after initialization of the device, look at `device.capture.channels` to get the actual channel count. So you basically have two options: 1) Pick an explicit channel count like "1" and let miniaudio do the conversion for you (it's safe to assume mono in that case); or 2) set the channel count to 0 and the conversion yourself. > However, if when I request mono from miniaudio, if that is always guaranteed to give me mono, then I am quite happy to make that assumption in my software as you suggest. Yes, this is guaranteed if you do `deviceConfig.capture.channels = 1`, and is what I would recommend.

title: Blocking on the main thread
last_maintainer_comment: Emscripten will always be a bit of a special case. The resource manager is multithreaded under the hood. When loading something synchronously what is actually happening is the loading is done on a background thread and then the calling thread waits (it's done like this to avoid having two separate code paths for synchronous and asynchronous loading). One option might be to call `ma_sound_init_*()` from a different thread. Another thing you could try is disabling threading with `MA_NO_THREADING` and then periodically call `ma_resource_manager_process_next_job()`, probably in your game loop. Another thing you could do is bypass the resource manager completely and just manage your own data sources and use `ma_sound_init_from_data_source()`, however that will be more work, and you'd miss out on the benefits of the resource manager. I have some plans to change the way sounds are loaded which *might* naturally address this but it's not ready yet, and Emscripten will need to be something I keep in mind when designing that. No promises or timeframes for that.

title: MSVC fails to compile
last_maintainer_comment: You can't include the implementation part of stb_vorbis before miniaudio's implementation. It's because miniaudio's `MA_VIRTUAL_AUDIO_DEVICE_PROCESS_LOOPBACK` is defined as this `L"VAD\\Process_Loopback"`. That `L` conflicts with stb_vorbis' definition of it: https://github.com/nothings/stb/blob/master/stb_vorbis.c#L5131 The solution is that either modify stb_vorbis, or put the stb_vorbis implementation after miniaudio's implementation. Also note that that stb_vorbis integration is being removed from miniaudio in a future version. This is not an error in miniaudio so closing this one.
